how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ssl_conf_command Options NoRenegotiation' in nginx or 'SSLRenegBufferSize 0' in Apache indicates client-initiated renegotiation is suppressed; absence of these directives means it is permitted by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh with renegotiation checks to determine whether the server accepts client-initiated renegotiation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Client-initiated Renegotiation: DoS threat' or 'VULNERABLE' indicates it is permitted; 'not vulnerable' confirms it is blocked at the server.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For HAProxy, check the 'no-tlsv10' and SSL bind options in the frontend configuration that control renegotiation behavior, and consult the HAProxy SSL termination documentation for the 'no-sslv3' bind option as a proxy for overall renegotiation posture.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HAProxy 2.0+ with 'ssl-options no-sslv3 no-tlsv10 no-tlsv11' and modern ciphers implicitly reduces renegotiation risk; explicit 'no-renegotiation' bind option in HAProxy 2.1+ directly disables client-initiated renegotiation.

option_description: Controls whether the TLS or application layer applies packet padding to normalize packet sizes, obscuring payload lengths and mitigating traffic analysis attacks that infer application behavior from packet size patterns.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'traffic_metadata_leakage_via_timing' exposure when both traffic_padding_enabled and traffic_shaping_or_dummy_traffic_enabled are false. Without padding, a passive observer can analyze packet size distributions to fingerprint encrypted traffic — for example, distinguishing login requests from file downloads, or identifying specific API calls by characteristic byte counts — even without decrypting the payload. This maps to MITRE T1040 (Network Sniffing) and T1001 (Data Obfuscation bypass).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the TLS server configuration for record_size_limit extension settings. In nginx, check for ssl_buffer_size directives; in HAProxy, look for tune.ssl.maxrecord; in OpenSSL-based configs, search for SSL_CTX_set_record_padding_callback or record_size_limit extension enablement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of ssl_buffer_size with a small fixed value (e.g., 1400 bytes), or record_size_limit extension configuration indicating padding is applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture live TLS traffic with tcpdump and analyze packet size variance using Wireshark or tshark. If padding is active, TLS records should cluster around uniform sizes rather than varying freely with payload size.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/tls_capture.pcap port 443 && tshark -r /tmp/tls_capture.pcap -T fields -e frame.len -e tls.record.length | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: With padding enabled, TLS record lengths appear clustered at fixed intervals (e.g., 512, 1024, 1448 bytes) rather than showing high variance correlating with application payload sizes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For QUIC-based endpoints (HTTP/3), query the application or gateway configuration API to check if PADDING frames are enabled. For Cloudflare or AWS CloudFront, inspect the TLS policy settings via the provider API.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN' 'https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/settings/tls_1_3' | jq '.result' && curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CF_API_TOKEN' 'https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/$ZONE_ID/settings' | jq '[.result[] | select(.id | test("padding|quic"))]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API response indicating padding or QUIC PADDING frame support is enabled in the zone or listener configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS Application Load Balancer console, navigate to EC2 > Load Balancers > select the ALB > Listeners tab, then review the Security Policy assigned. For Nginx Plus or F5 BIG-IP, check the SSL profile configuration under Local Traffic > Profiles > SSL > Client for record-layer padding options.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > [ALB Name] > Listeners > Security Policy details; F5 BIG-IP: Local Traffic > Profiles > SSL > Client > [Profile Name] > Record Layer settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Security policy or SSL profile showing a fixed or bounded record size setting indicating normalization of packet sizes.

typical_values: false (most common — padding is rarely enabled in standard deployments)
true (seen in high-security VPN gateways, Tor-adjacent infrastructure, or QUIC implementations with padding frames enabled)

option_description: Controls whether the system injects dummy or cover traffic, or enforces constant-bitrate traffic shaping on the encrypted channel, to mask real traffic timing patterns and flow durations from passive observers performing traffic analysis.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'traffic_metadata_leakage_via_timing' exposure when both this attribute and traffic_padding_enabled are false. Even with strong encryption, a passive adversary monitoring inter-packet timing and session duration can infer session activity — identifying idle vs. active periods, correlating communication events, or fingerprinting specific workflows. Cover traffic eliminates these side channels. This is especially critical for high-assurance remote access scenarios where adversaries monitor network metadata (T1040, T1001).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect VPN gateway configuration files for chaff traffic, cover traffic, or constant-bitrate tunnel settings. In OpenVPN, look for the 'tls-auth' and keepalive directives used for dummy traffic; in WireGuard configurations, check for PersistentKeepalive settings and any traffic shaping wrappers. For enterprise VPN appliances (Palo Alto GlobalProtect, Cisco AnyConnect), review tunnel profile configurations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries showing constant keepalive intervals sending traffic regardless of real session activity, or explicit cover-traffic/shaping directives.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Palo Alto Panorama or the NGFW web interface, navigate to Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways > [Gateway Name] > Agent > Tunnel Settings and check for 'Tunnel Monitor' or traffic shaping profiles. For Cisco AnyConnect, review the VPN Profile Editor under Preferences for traffic normalization settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Palo Alto: Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways > [Name] > Agent > Tunnel Settings; Cisco ASDM: Configuration > Remote Access VPN > Network (Client) Access > AnyConnect Connection Profiles > [Profile] > Advanced
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Traffic shaping or constant-rate transmission policy applied to the tunnel profile, or explicit dummy-traffic generation settings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Monitor inter-packet arrival times on an established VPN or TLS session during an idle period. If cover traffic is active, packets should continue arriving at regular intervals even with no real user activity.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/vpn_idle.pcap port 443 or port 1194 or port 51820 & sleep 60; kill %1; tshark -r /tmp/vpn_idle.pcap -T fields -e frame.time_relative -e frame.len | awk 'NR>1{print $1, $2}' | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: With cover traffic enabled, packets appear at regular fixed intervals (e.g., every 10–15 seconds) even during idle periods. Without it, the capture shows silence during idle periods.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network security team or review the VPN/proxy deployment runbook to determine whether traffic shaping policies or cover-traffic generation were intentionally configured. Check change management records for QoS or traffic normalization policy deployments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or staff confirmation that a traffic shaping policy or dummy-traffic mechanism was deliberately implemented on the remote access infrastructure, with the specific technology identified.

typical_values: false (almost universal default — cover traffic is computationally and bandwidth expensive and rarely deployed)
true (observed in intelligence community networks, high-assurance government VPNs, and specialized anonymity infrastructure)
